title: Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl
full_review:
There was a time when theme-park rides were based on summer blockbuster movies. Yet in Hollywood's most recent original idea drought, Tinseltown, when not pillaging old TV series or plundering comic books, has turned to pirating theme-park rides for inspiration.

Based on the popular Disney animatronic attraction, "Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl" (Disney) is an entertaining high seas romp. It's like being a kid again and playing Errol Flynn, only this time you have Michael Eisner's platinum American Express card to buy some really cool props.
Paying lighthearted homage to such films as "Treasure Island" (1950) and Flynn's "Captain Blood" (1935), Gore Verbinski's popcorn pirate yarn is full of shiver-me-timber fun, despite cardboard characters and a story line that flaunts a self-parodying silliness.

With a price tag that could have some Disney execs walking the proverbial plank, the film's unabashed escapism -- most evident in the tongue-in-cheek choreography of its sprawling naval battles and at times tedious swashbuckling duels -- should save this ship from sinking to what might otherwise have been the box-office equivalent of Davy Jones' locker.

The film opens with a British frigate bound for the Caribbean destination of Port Royal. On board are the island's newly appointed governor (Jonathan Pryce), and his precocious daughter, Elizabeth. While en route, they encounter a merchant ship in flames, courtesy of the skull and crossbones. They pull the vessel's sole survivor, a barely conscious lad named Will Turner, from the wreckage. The boy is clutching a gold doubloon adorned with strange carvings. Fascinated by the curious coin, Elizabeth swipes it.

The action then fast-forwards several years. Elizabeth (Keira Knightley), now grown up, still lives with her father on the island, keeping her exotic souvenir safely tucked away. Though betrothed to the priggish Commodore Norrington (Jack Davenport), she secretly harbors feelings for Will (Orlando Bloom), who has matured into a dashing but lowly blacksmith with a knack for swordplay, prohibited by his menial station from expressing his true emotions for the aristocratic Elizabeth.

Enter Captain Jack Sparrow (Johnny Depp), the greatest pirate ever to roam the Spanish Main. In one of recent cinema's more comical entrees, the rum-soaked rogue stumbles into Port Royal and is soon arrested by Norrington, who sentences him to "a short drop and a sudden stop."

But the hangman's noose is cut short when Sparrow's ex-first mate and now nemesis, Captain Barbossa (Geoffrey Rush), sails into town, cannons firing, aboard the infamous Black Pearl. It is later learned that Barbossa, a pirate so nefarious that "hell spit him back out," had stolen the Black Pearl from Sparrow.
Along with his mutinous crew, Barbossa had plundered many treasures, including a chest of "Aztec gold" upon which the heathen gods had placed a curse, condemning him and his men to forever roam the seas as undead souls -- revealed by moonlight to be skeletons in various stages of decomposition.

The spell cannot be broken until they restore the damned loot in full and a blood-debt is repaid. The ghostly pirates have recovered all the gold pieces except the one dangling from the chain around Elizabeth's lovely neck.

When Barbossa's patch-eyed posse kidnaps Elizabeth, Will enlists the aid of Sparrow, and a rag-tag crew of seafaring misfits in order to save her. With Norrington hot in pursuit, the comical corsairs commandeer the fastest clipper in the British fleet, the HMS Interceptor, and set a course for the Isla de Muerta to cross swords with Barbossa and his blackhearted buccaneers.

Though the cartoonish characters rarely warrant more acting range than the animatronic pirates on which they are based, the movie is well-paced, calibrated with an equal measure of action and humor. In fact, much of the fun is generated by the film's playful burlesquing of established pirate cliches and a whimsical ability to avoid taking itself too seriously.

The beard-braided Depp, who slurs much of his dialogue as if in a permanent Jamaican rum stupor, is mesmerizing as the quirky, yet charming scallywag.

Parents should be advised that the movie contains some scary scenes which may prove disturbing to young children. The film's violence, which for the most part involves swordplay -- though there are several gallows sequences -- is handled in a lighthearted manner. A scattering of corset jokes is in keeping with the spirit of salty pirate humor and doesn't approach anything of a risque sexual nature.

For those landlubbers who want to venture into deep dramatic waters, let this pirate ship pass you by. But for those who don't mind dropping anchor in the narrative shallows, "Pirates of the Caribbean" may offer some welcome yo-ho-ho's and a bottle of fun.
Due to recurring action/adventure violence, some frightening supernatural effects and mildly lewd humor, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
